### Three runs worth doing (they exercise the distinct paths)

| Command | What it demonstrates |
|---|---|
| `python src/graph.py --manifest M001 --tag pass` | Clear **PASS** (79.41% vs 40%) |
| `python src/graph.py --manifest M009 --tag fail` | Clear **FAIL** (10.66% vs 45%) |
| `python src/graph.py --manifest M005 --tag borderline` | **BORDERLINE** (51.00% vs 50%) — answer `approve` to see the borderline warning carried into the report |
| `python src/graph.py --manifest M010 --tag override` | **CLASSIFICATION_UNAVAILABLE** — answer `edit` to supply an HS code and watch the recalculation loop |

### Regenerating the trajectory logs without a terminal

The committed trajectories in `logs/trajectories/` were produced with `--decision`,
which answers the checkpoint from the command line so the logs are reproducible by
anyone:

```bash
python src/graph.py --manifest M001 --tag pass       --decision approve
python src/graph.py --manifest M009 --tag fail       --decision approve
python src/graph.py --manifest M005 --tag borderline --decision reject
python src/graph.py --manifest M010 --tag declined   --decision reject
```

Note what `reject` demonstrates: **no report file is produced at all.** On M005 that is a
reviewer declining to certify a 51.00%-against-50% borderline without further
documentation. On M010 it is the correct outcome — the product is a solar PV module
(HS 8541.43), no rule in the controlled set covers it, and the right answer is to
decline rather than to substitute an adjacent code. The baseline substituted `8544.42`
here; a reviewer should not repeat that.

The panel still renders, state is still checkpointed before the decision, and
`GENERATE_REPORT` is still reachable only through an explicit approve. What changes is
**who answers** — and the flag writes that into `human_notes`, so a trajectory produced
this way says `SCRIPTED DECISION ... This was not a human sign-off` on its face. The
interactive prompt is the default and the only path a real user takes.

A reviewer cannot use `--edit-hs-code` to introduce a code outside the dataset; the run
exits rather than accepting it, exactly as the interactive path does.
input.new_string:
### Four runs worth doing (they exercise the distinct paths)

| Command | What it demonstrates |
|---|---|
| `python src/graph.py --manifest M001 --tag pass` | Clear **PASS** (79.41% vs 40%) |
| `python src/graph.py --manifest M009 --tag fail` | Clear **FAIL** (10.66% vs 45%) |
| `python src/graph.py --manifest M005 --tag borderline` | **BORDERLINE** (51.00% vs 50%) — answer `approve` to see the borderline warning carried into the report |
| `python src/graph.py --manifest M010 --tag declined` | **The most informative run.** Answer `reject`. See below — this is the case the automated guards miss |

**What M010 actually does, and why it is in this table.** M010 is a solar photovoltaic
module. Its correct classification is HS 8541.43, which is **deliberately absent** from
the controlled dataset, so the correct outcome is `CLASSIFICATION_UNAVAILABLE` and a
referral to a human.

That is not what happens. The model proposes `8544.42` — insulated electrical
conductors, an adjacent rule that **is** in the table — so the membership guard passes it
through, and you will watch the run print a confident `8544.42 / 12.31% / FAIL` with a
self-reported confidence of `1.00` and **zero** verification warnings. Nothing automated
catches it. The only thing that does is you, reading "photovoltaic module" beside
"insulated electric conductors" on the panel and typing `reject`.

Run this one. It is the case where the human checkpoint stops being a compliance
formality and starts being the actual control. See README's "Structural guarantees" and
CHANGELOG's "The HS guard is narrower than I had claimed".

### Regenerating the trajectory logs without a terminal

The committed trajectories in `logs/trajectories/` were produced with `--decision`,
which answers the checkpoint from the command line so the logs are reproducible by
anyone:

```bash
python src/graph.py --manifest M001 --tag pass       --decision approve
python src/graph.py --manifest M009 --tag fail       --decision approve
python src/graph.py --manifest M005 --tag borderline --decision approve
python src/graph.py --manifest M010 --tag declined   --decision reject
```

Those four commands produce exactly the four logs in the repository. The first three
approve and therefore each write a draft report; **M010 rejects and produces no report
file at all**, which is the point of including it.

**Why there is no `edit` trajectory, stated plainly.** The reviewer's edit path is real
and bounded, but no manifest in this dataset offers a *legitimate* edit to demonstrate.
The agent classified 9 of 10 correctly, so editing any of those would mean introducing an
error; and on M010 the correct code (8541.43) is not in the dataset by design, so the only
edit available there is the adjacent wrong code the guard exists to catch. Rather than
ship a demonstration that teaches the wrong lesson, the edit loop is proven by test:
`tests/test_checkpoint.py::test_an_edit_triggers_a_genuine_recalculation` asserts that an
edit produces a **second** `CALCULATE_RVC` event against the new threshold rather than
relabelling the first result, and a companion test asserts the loop is bounded at
`MAX_EDIT_ROUNDS`.

You can still see the edit guard refuse an out-of-dataset code, which takes seconds and
needs no model:

```bash
python src/graph.py --manifest M001 --decision edit --edit-hs-code 9999.99
```

It exits with the list of codes the controlled dataset actually contains. A reviewer
cannot introduce a code the rule table does not have — the same restriction the
interactive path enforces.

The panel still renders, state is still checkpointed before the decision, and
`GENERATE_REPORT` is still reachable only through an explicit approve. What changes is
**who answers** — and the flag writes that into `human_notes`, so a trajectory produced
this way says `SCRIPTED DECISION ... This was not a human sign-off` on its face. The
interactive prompt is the default and the only path a real user takes.

# REPRODUCTION

Exact commands for a clean environment. Windows paths shown; the POSIX equivalents
are noted where they differ.

## 0. Prerequisites

- **Python 3.11+** (developed and measured on 3.14.7)
- **[Ollama](https://ollama.com)** running locally
- ~5 GB free disk for the model
- No API key. No account. No network calls to any third party — the model runs on
  your machine and the rule data is a local JSON file.

## 1. Install the model

```bash
ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b
ollama serve          # if not already running as a service
```

Confirm it is reachable:

```bash
ollama list
```

> **Note on the model.** The build brief specified Qwen 2.5 7B *instruct*. Only the
> **coder** variant was available on the build machine, and pulling the instruct
> variant metered at 387 KB/s with a 3h11m ETA — not affordable inside the build
> window. All reported results are from `qwen2.5-coder:7b`. See CHANGELOG.
>
> To run against a different model instead, set `NAVIGATOR_LOCAL_MODEL` (below).
> No code change is required.

## 2. Set up the environment

**Windows (PowerShell):**
```powershell
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

**macOS / Linux:**
```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

## 3. Environment variables (all optional)

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `OLLAMA_HOST` | `http://localhost:11434` | Where Ollama is listening |
| `NAVIGATOR_LOCAL_MODEL` | `qwen2.5-coder:7b` | The model used for all three LLM nodes |
| `NAVIGATOR_CLOUD_MODEL` | `qwen3.5:cloud` | Escalation target. **Not used by default** — no node demonstrated a need for it |
| `NAVIGATOR_TIMEOUT_S` | `300` | Per-request timeout |

Nothing needs to be set for a default run.

## 4. Verify the deterministic core first

This needs **no model and no network**. Run it before anything else — if this fails,
nothing downstream is trustworthy.

```bash
python -m pytest tests/ -q
```

**Expected:** `119 passed` in about two seconds.

This covers the RVC arithmetic, the rule lookup, origin resolution, the borderline
band, a re-derivation of every ground-truth figure in the dataset from its own bill of
materials, the report's figure isolation, and the human checkpoint's control flow. The
last two stub the model out entirely: the report tests feed it a deliberately hostile
narrative (fabricated percentages, fabricated costs, a contradicted verdict) and assert
the assessment block is unmoved; the checkpoint tests run the whole workflow with a
scripted reviewer and assert no input can reach `GENERATE_REPORT` without an approve.

## 5. Run the baseline

```bash
python src/baseline.py
```

Single manifest instead:
```bash
python src/baseline.py --manifest M005
```

**Expected output shape:**
```
Baseline: qwen2.5-coder:7b | 10 manifest(s) | zero-shot, no tools

  M001 ... 1806.32 | 47.5% | PASS | MISMATCH | 45.3s
  ...
```

**Measured runtime:** ~**378 s total**, ~**37.8 s per case**, **1 model call per case**.
**Measured cost:** **$0.00** — local inference, no API billing. The real cost is
latency and local compute.

Writes `logs/baseline_results.json`.

## 6. Run the full workflow (this is where the human interrupt fires)

```bash
python src/graph.py --manifest M005
```

Available manifests:
```bash
python src/graph.py --list
```

The run prints each node as it completes, then **stops** and waits for you:

```
  HUMAN REVIEW REQUIRED — execution is paused
  ...
  RVC             : 51.00%  vs threshold 50.00%   (+1.00 pp)
                    ^ inside the +/-2.0pp borderline band
  STATUS          : BORDERLINE

  [approve] issue the draft report with these findings
  [reject]  stop; do not issue a report
  [edit]    correct the HS code, then recalculate

  Your decision (approve/reject/edit):
```

Type `approve`, `reject`, or `edit` and press Enter. **Nothing is generated until you
answer** — `GENERATE_REPORT` is unreachable except through an explicit `approve`.

State is written to `logs/checkpoints/<id>.checkpoint.json` *before* the pause, so
the interrupt survives process exit.

Your own manifest, from a file or a pipe:
```bash
python src/graph.py --file my_manifest.txt
cat my_manifest.txt | python src/graph.py --stdin
```

Each run writes a full trajectory log to `logs/trajectories/`.

### Three runs worth doing (they exercise the distinct paths)

| Command | What it demonstrates |
|---|---|
| `python src/graph.py --manifest M001 --tag pass` | Clear **PASS** (79.41% vs 40%) |
| `python src/graph.py --manifest M009 --tag fail` | Clear **FAIL** (10.66% vs 45%) |
| `python src/graph.py --manifest M005 --tag borderline` | **BORDERLINE** (51.00% vs 50%) — answer `approve` to see the borderline warning carried into the report |
| `python src/graph.py --manifest M010 --tag override` | **CLASSIFICATION_UNAVAILABLE** — answer `edit` to supply an HS code and watch the recalculation loop |

### Regenerating the trajectory logs without a terminal

The committed trajectories in `logs/trajectories/` were produced with `--decision`,
which answers the checkpoint from the command line so the logs are reproducible by
anyone:

```bash
python src/graph.py --manifest M001 --tag pass       --decision approve
python src/graph.py --manifest M009 --tag fail       --decision approve
python src/graph.py --manifest M005 --tag borderline --decision reject
python src/graph.py --manifest M010 --tag declined   --decision reject
```

Note what `reject` demonstrates: **no report file is produced at all.** On M005 that is a
reviewer declining to certify a 51.00%-against-50% borderline without further
documentation. On M010 it is the correct outcome — the product is a solar PV module
(HS 8541.43), no rule in the controlled set covers it, and the right answer is to
decline rather than to substitute an adjacent code. The baseline substituted `8544.42`
here; a reviewer should not repeat that.

The panel still renders, state is still checkpointed before the decision, and
`GENERATE_REPORT` is still reachable only through an explicit approve. What changes is
**who answers** — and the flag writes that into `human_notes`, so a trajectory produced
this way says `SCRIPTED DECISION ... This was not a human sign-off` on its face. The
interactive prompt is the default and the only path a real user takes.

A reviewer cannot use `--edit-hs-code` to introduce a code outside the dataset; the run
exits rather than accepting it, exactly as the interactive path does.

## 7. Run the comparison

```bash
python eval/run_comparison.py
```

To reuse the baseline results already on disk rather than re-running them:
```bash
python eval/run_comparison.py --reuse-baseline
```

**Runtime:** the agent side makes 2 model calls per case, so budget roughly
**double the baseline's per-case latency**. Full 10-case comparison from cold:
~15–20 minutes. With `--reuse-baseline`: ~8–10 minutes.

**Cost:** **$0.00** for both systems. Both run on local Ollama; there is no API
charge to report. The workflow makes *more* model calls than the baseline
(2/case vs 1/case) — that is a genuine cost of the architecture, not a hidden
advantage.

Writes `logs/comparison_results.json` and prints a per-manifest table plus a
scorecard.

## 8. Timing notes (measured, not estimated)

- **First call after `ollama serve` takes ~25 s** even for a two-token reply — that
  is the model loading into memory, not inference. Subsequent calls on this machine
  ran 33–45 s for real work.
- Timings above are from a Windows 11 machine running the 7B model on local
  hardware. Yours will differ; the *relative* comparison between the two systems is
  what the evaluation is about.
- Deterministic nodes (`LOOKUP_RULE`, `CALCULATE_RVC`, `VERIFY`) run in
  **single-digit milliseconds** and appear as such in the trajectory logs.

"""


_NUMERIC_PATTERN = re.compile(r"\d+(?:[.,]\d+)?\s*%|(?:USD|\$)\s*[\d,]+(?:\.\d+)?")


def _scan_for_invented_figures(narrative: dict[str, Any]) -> list[str]:
    """Flag any figure the model wrote into prose.

    The report's numeric fields are assembled from state, so a number appearing in
    the narrative cannot change the assessment -- but it can mislead a reader. The
    prompt forbids figures; this check verifies the prompt was obeyed instead of
    assuming it. A hit is recorded in the report metadata rather than silently
    dropped, because "the model ignored the instruction" is worth knowing.
    """
    hits: list[str] = []
    for field, value in narrative.items():
        text = " ".join(value) if isinstance(value, list) else str(value)
        for match in _NUMERIC_PATTERN.findall(text):
            hits.append(f"{field}: {match.strip()}")
    return hits


def node_generate_report(state: NavigatorState, model: str = LOCAL_MODEL) -> NavigatorState:
    """Assemble the final document. Numbers come from state; the LLM writes prose only.

    The structure is the enforcement mechanism. ``assessment`` is built from state
    fields in this function, and the model's output is confined to ``narrative``.
    There is no code path by which a model token becomes a reported figure.
    """
    started = time.perf_counter()
    result = call_model(
        _report_prompt(state), model=model, system=REPORT_SYSTEM, json_mode=True, temperature=0.2
    )
    elapsed = (time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000.0

    payload = parse_json_text(result.text) or {}

    def _text(key: str) -> str:
        """Coerce a narrative field to a string, treating JSON null as absent.

        ``str(None)`` is ``"None"`` -- truthy, and it would sail past the
        ``narrative_ok`` check straight into the document as the summary. Caught by
        tests/test_report_integrity.py.
        """
        value = payload.get(key)
        return "" if value is None else str(value).strip()

    narrative = {
        "summary": _text("summary"),
        "what_this_means": _text("what_this_means"),
        "recommended_next_steps": [
            str(s).strip()
            for s in (payload.get("recommended_next_steps") or [])
            if s is not None and str(s).strip()
        ],
        "limitations": _text("limitations"),
    }
    narrative_ok = bool(narrative["summary"])
    invented = _scan_for_invented_figures(narrative)

_NUMERIC_PATTERN = re.compile(r"\d+(?:[.,]\d+)?\s*%|(?:USD|\$)\s*[\d,]+(?:\.\d+)?")

# Affirmative assurances the narrative must never make. The prompt already forbids

# contradicted the disclaimer printed directly beneath it. The prompt was a request;
# this is the check. See CHANGELOG.
#
# Only affirmative constructions are listed. Bare words like "legal" or "certified"
# are deliberately absent, because the narrative is *asked* for a limitations
# sentence saying this is "not a legal determination" and flagging that would train
# the reader to ignore the flag.
_OVERCLAIM_PATTERNS: list[tuple[re.Pattern[str], str]] = [
    (re.compile(r"without any (?:issues|problems|restrictions|barriers)", re.I),
     "unqualified assurance"),
    (re.compile(r"\bno (?:issues|problems|barriers|restrictions)\b", re.I),
     "unqualified assurance"),
    (re.compile(r"\b(?:you (?:can|may) now|free to)\s+(?:export|ship|file|claim)", re.I),
     "grants a permission this system cannot grant"),
    (re.compile(r"\b(?:is|are)\s+(?:now\s+)?(?:legally\s+)?"
                r"(?:certified|approved|cleared|authoris\w+|authoriz\w+)\b", re.I),
     "asserts a decision only an authority can make"),
    (re.compile(r"\bwill (?:be )?(?:accepted|approved|cleared)\b", re.I),
     "predicts an authority's decision"),
    (re.compile(r"\bguarantee(?:s|d|ing)?\b", re.I), "guarantee"),
    (re.compile(r"\bfully compliant\b|\bcompliant with all\b", re.I),
     "unqualified compliance claim"),
    (re.compile(r"\bduty[-\s]free\b", re.I), "asserts a tariff outcome"),
    (re.compile(r"\blegally binding\b", re.I), "asserts legal force"),
    (re.compile(r"\bcertificate of origin\b", re.I), "names a document this is not"),
]

# "This is NOT a certificate of origin" is the correct sentence, so a match whose
# immediately preceding text negates it is not a hit.
_NEGATION_BEFORE = re.compile(r"\b(?:not|no|never|cannot|can't|isn't|aren't|without)\b[^.]{0,40}$", re.I)

    return hits

    """Flag prose that asserts legal standing this assessment does not have.

    The figure scan protects the *numbers*; nothing protected the *claims*. The
    narrative is generated after the human has already approved the assessment, so
    an overclaim reaches the document without any reviewer ever reading it. This
    scan is what makes that visible.

    Known limits, stated rather than implied: it is a phrase list, so it catches the
    constructions observed in real runs and paraphrases close to them, not every
    possible way of overstating a result. It bounds recognised phrasings, not
    meaning -- the same distinction the HS membership guard runs into.

    hits: list[str] = []
    for field, value in narrative.items():
        text = " ".join(value) if isinstance(value, list) else str(value)

                if _NEGATION_BEFORE.search(text[: match.start()]):
                    continue
                hits.append(f"{field}: {match.group(0).strip()!r} — {why}")
    return hits

# REPRODUCTION

Exact commands for a clean environment. Windows paths shown; the POSIX equivalents
are noted where they differ.

## 0. Prerequisites

- **Python 3.11+** (developed and measured on 3.14.7)
- **[Ollama](https://ollama.com)** running locally
- ~5 GB free disk for the model
- No API key. No account. No network calls to any third party — the model runs on
  your machine and the rule data is a local JSON file.

## 1. Install the model

```bash
ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b
ollama serve          # if not already running as a service
```

Confirm it is reachable:

```bash
ollama list
```

> **Note on the model.** The build brief specified Qwen 2.5 7B *instruct*. Only the
> **coder** variant was available on the build machine, and pulling the instruct
> variant metered at 387 KB/s with a 3h11m ETA — not affordable inside the build
> window. All reported results are from `qwen2.5-coder:7b`. See CHANGELOG.
>
> To run against a different model instead, set `NAVIGATOR_LOCAL_MODEL` (below).
> No code change is required.

## 2. Set up the environment

**Windows (PowerShell):**
```powershell
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

**macOS / Linux:**
```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

## 3. Environment variables (all optional)

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `OLLAMA_HOST` | `http://localhost:11434` | Where Ollama is listening |
| `NAVIGATOR_LOCAL_MODEL` | `qwen2.5-coder:7b` | The model used for all three LLM nodes |
| `NAVIGATOR_CLOUD_MODEL` | `qwen3.5:cloud` | Escalation target. **Not used by default** — no node demonstrated a need for it |
| `NAVIGATOR_TIMEOUT_S` | `300` | Per-request timeout |

Nothing needs to be set for a default run.

## 4. Verify the deterministic core first

This needs **no model and no network**. Run it before anything else — if this fails,
nothing downstream is trustworthy.

```bash
python -m pytest tests/ -q
```

**Expected:** `119 passed` in about two seconds.

This covers the RVC arithmetic, the rule lookup, origin resolution, the borderline
band, a re-derivation of every ground-truth figure in the dataset from its own bill of
materials, the report's figure isolation, and the human checkpoint's control flow. The
last two stub the model out entirely: the report tests feed it a deliberately hostile
narrative (fabricated percentages, fabricated costs, a contradicted verdict) and assert
the assessment block is unmoved; the checkpoint tests run the whole workflow with a
scripted reviewer and assert no input can reach `GENERATE_REPORT` without an approve.

## 5. Run the baseline

```bash
python src/baseline.py
```

Single manifest instead:
```bash
python src/baseline.py --manifest M005
```

**Expected output shape:**
```
Baseline: qwen2.5-coder:7b | 10 manifest(s) | zero-shot, no tools

  M001 ... 1806.32 | 47.5% | PASS | MISMATCH | 45.3s
  ...
```

**Measured runtime:** ~**378 s total**, ~**37.8 s per case**, **1 model call per case**.
**Measured cost:** **$0.00** — local inference, no API billing. The real cost is
latency and local compute.

Writes `logs/baseline_results.json`.

## 6. Run the full workflow (this is where the human interrupt fires)

```bash
python src/graph.py --manifest M005
```

Available manifests:
```bash
python src/graph.py --list
```

The run prints each node as it completes, then **stops** and waits for you:

```
  HUMAN REVIEW REQUIRED — execution is paused
  ...
  RVC             : 51.00%  vs threshold 50.00%   (+1.00 pp)
                    ^ inside the +/-2.0pp borderline band
  STATUS          : BORDERLINE

  [approve] issue the draft report with these findings
  [reject]  stop; do not issue a report
  [edit]    correct the HS code, then recalculate

  Your decision (approve/reject/edit):
```

Type `approve`, `reject`, or `edit` and press Enter. **Nothing is generated until you
answer** — `GENERATE_REPORT` is unreachable except through an explicit `approve`.

State is written to `logs/checkpoints/<id>.checkpoint.json` *before* the pause, so
the interrupt survives process exit.

Your own manifest, from a file or a pipe:
```bash
python src/graph.py --file my_manifest.txt
cat my_manifest.txt | python src/graph.py --stdin
```

Each run writes a full trajectory log to `logs/trajectories/`.

### Four runs worth doing (they exercise the distinct paths)

| Command | What it demonstrates |
|---|---|
| `python src/graph.py --manifest M001 --tag pass` | Clear **PASS** (79.41% vs 40%) |
| `python src/graph.py --manifest M009 --tag fail` | Clear **FAIL** (10.66% vs 45%) |
| `python src/graph.py --manifest M005 --tag borderline` | **BORDERLINE** (51.00% vs 50%) — answer `approve` to see the borderline warning carried into the report |
| `python src/graph.py --manifest M010 --tag declined` | **The most informative run.** Answer `reject`. See below — this is the case the automated guards miss |

**What M010 actually does, and why it is in this table.** M010 is a solar photovoltaic
module. Its correct classification is HS 8541.43, which is **deliberately absent** from
the controlled dataset, so the correct outcome is `CLASSIFICATION_UNAVAILABLE` and a
referral to a human.

That is not what happens. The model proposes `8544.42` — insulated electrical
conductors, an adjacent rule that **is** in the table — so the membership guard passes it
through, and you will watch the run print a confident `8544.42 / 12.31% / FAIL` with a
self-reported confidence of `1.00` and **zero** verification warnings. Nothing automated
catches it. The only thing that does is you, reading "photovoltaic module" beside
"insulated electric conductors" on the panel and typing `reject`.

Run this one. It is the case where the human checkpoint stops being a compliance
formality and starts being the actual control. See README's "Structural guarantees" and
CHANGELOG's "The HS guard is narrower than I had claimed".

### Regenerating the trajectory logs without a terminal

The committed trajectories in `logs/trajectories/` were produced with `--decision`,
which answers the checkpoint from the command line so the logs are reproducible by
anyone:

```bash
python src/graph.py --manifest M001 --tag pass       --decision approve
python src/graph.py --manifest M009 --tag fail       --decision approve
python src/graph.py --manifest M005 --tag borderline --decision approve
python src/graph.py --manifest M010 --tag declined   --decision reject
```

Those four commands produce exactly the four logs in the repository. The first three
approve and therefore each write a draft report; **M010 rejects and produces no report
file at all**, which is the point of including it.

**Why there is no `edit` trajectory, stated plainly.** The reviewer's edit path is real
and bounded, but no manifest in this dataset offers a *legitimate* edit to demonstrate.
The agent classified 9 of 10 correctly, so editing any of those would mean introducing an
error; and on M010 the correct code (8541.43) is not in the dataset by design, so the only
edit available there is the adjacent wrong code the guard exists to catch. Rather than
ship a demonstration that teaches the wrong lesson, the edit loop is proven by test:
`tests/test_checkpoint.py::test_an_edit_triggers_a_genuine_recalculation` asserts that an
edit produces a **second** `CALCULATE_RVC` event against the new threshold rather than
relabelling the first result, and a companion test asserts the loop is bounded at
`MAX_EDIT_ROUNDS`.

You can still see the edit guard refuse an out-of-dataset code, which takes seconds and
needs no model:

```bash
python src/graph.py --manifest M001 --decision edit --edit-hs-code 9999.99
```

It exits with the list of codes the controlled dataset actually contains. A reviewer
cannot introduce a code the rule table does not have — the same restriction the
interactive path enforces.

The panel still renders, state is still checkpointed before the decision, and
`GENERATE_REPORT` is still reachable only through an explicit approve. What changes is
**who answers** — and the flag writes that into `human_notes`, so a trajectory produced
this way says `SCRIPTED DECISION ... This was not a human sign-off` on its face. The
interactive prompt is the default and the only path a real user takes.

## DO NOT BUILD A UI

Asked and answered: **no.** Reasons, in order of weight:

1. **The rubric has no UI points.** 100 points across Problem & User Value 15, Agent
   Solution & Engineering 30, End to End Quality 20, Measured Improvement 15,
   Reproducibility 15, Hot Take 5. "End to End Quality" is about work someone would sign
   their name to — the draft report, the docs and the evidence trail already carry that.
2. **The missing deliverable is the video, not a frontend.** Time spent on Django/Next.js
   is time not spent on the one thing that is actually absent.
3. **A hosted UI destroys the product's best property.** Right now the model is local: the
   exporter's confidential costings never leave their machine, and marginal cost is
   $0.00. Put it behind a web app and you need a server running a 7B model, and the
   privacy story and the cost story both evaporate.
4. **Your own build spec said so** — "Explicitly NO frontend now — a clean CLI is enough
   for judging; the video needs realistic execution, not UI."

### If you build it *after* the hackathon: honest estimate

The seams are already right — `run_pipeline_to_verify` is separated from the human step,
`decision_provider` is an injectable callable, and rules/origins are data behind typed
interfaces. So this is building a web layer, not rewriting the core.

| Work | Hours |
|---|---|
| Django + DRF scaffold, settings, CORS | 1–2 |
| Job queue (Celery + Redis) — mandatory, the pipeline is ~97 s and cannot sit in a request | 3–4 |
| Persist `NavigatorState` to the DB, models + migrations (replaces the disk checkpoint) | 2–3 |
| **Split `run_assessment` into run→pause→resume-from-decision** — the real refactor | 3–4 |
| Two-phase review API: POST start → poll status → POST decision | 2–3 |
| Auth + user scoping | 3–4 |
| API tests | 3–4 |
| **Backend subtotal** | **17–24** |
| Next.js scaffold, routing, API client | 2–3 |
| Manifest input (paste / upload) | 2–3 |
| Progress view for the ~97 s run (polling or SSE) | 3–4 |
| **The review panel** — BOM line by line, origins, totals, threshold, margin, warnings, 3 actions. Most important screen in the product; M010 proves it is the actual control | 5–7 |
| Report view + print/PDF | 3–4 |
| Loading / error / empty states, responsive | 3–4 |
| **Frontend subtotal** | **18–25** |
| Deployment: Docker, env config, **and somewhere to run the 7B model** | 6–10 |
| **TOTAL** | **~41–59 h** |

Call it **1 focused week full-time, or 2–3 weeks part-time**, for a competent build — not
a polished one. The unlisted risk is item 3 above: hosting means either provisioning GPU
capacity or switching to a paid API, which changes the product's economics.

**Cheaper middle path if you ever want something visual:** a single-page FastAPI + HTMX
version reusing the existing Python directly, ~8–12 h. Still not worth doing before this

Added `known_external_origins` to the data file and a regression test (`test_routine_imports_do_not_raise_a_review_flag`). **This node changed because of an observed problem, not a predicted one.** |
| **Origin alias layer justified itself** | Added fuzzy origin matching (aliases, "City, Country", embedded country names) as cheap defence. | The live extraction returned **"Ivory Coast"**, not the dataset's "Cote d'Ivoire". Without the alias map, M001's RVC would have silently dropped from 79.41% to 54.9% and still looked plausible. | Kept. A silently-wrong percentage is this product's worst failure mode, so defence at the origin boundary is worth its ~30 lines. |
| **GENERATE_REPORT: structure over instruction** | Could have asked the model to restate the figures accurately. | The baseline's whole failure mode is confident fabricated numbers. | The report's numeric fields are **assembled from state in Python**; the model writes only named prose fields. There is no code path from a model token to a reported figure. A regex scan additionally flags any figure it writes into prose, so "the model ignored the instruction" is recorded rather than assumed away. |
| **Cold start measured** | First call took ~25s for a 2-token reply. | Subsequent calls 33–45s for real work. | Cold model load is real and reported honestly in REPRODUCTION.md rather than hidden by warming the model before timing. |
| **Two eval runs raced each other** | Relaunched the comparison after the first run's task handle was lost mid-session, assuming it had died. | It had not. Both processes were alive and competing for the same local model. The orphan finished first and wrote a complete 10-row result file; **agent per-case latency climbed monotonically 105s → 263s across the run**, which is contention, not workload. | Killed the duplicate, preserved the contaminated file as `logs/comparison_results_contended.json`, and re-measured with nothing else running. **Accuracy figures were unaffected** (temperature 0, same prompts, deterministic tools) but the latency figures were worthless and would have been reported as real. Checking that a background process is actually dead is cheaper than the retraction. |
| **Cloud escalation NOT enabled** | Spec allows escalating to `qwen3.5:cloud` where the local model struggles. | Local model scored **9/10 on HS classification** and produced usable report prose. | **Not enabled.** No node demonstrated a need. The env var `NAVIGATOR_CLOUD_MODEL` makes escalation a one-line change if evidence later appears, but shipping it now would be complexity without a cause. |
| **1.5B model not used** | Available on disk. | No experiment gave a reason to introduce a third model. | Unused, and therefore not claimed as part of the architecture. |
| **Human checkpoint is structural** | Could have made approval a flag. | — | `GENERATE_REPORT` is unreachable except through an explicit `approve` decision, and state is checkpointed to disk before the pause so the interrupt survives process exit. The evaluation harness stops at `VERIFY` and does **not** simulate the human, so no accuracy number is credited to a scripted approval. |
| **`--list` was broken** | Documented `python src/graph.py --list` in REPRODUCTION.md, then ran it. | `error: one of the arguments --manifest --file --stdin is required` — argparse enforced the required source group before control ever reached the `--list` branch. | Made the source group optional and enforced the requirement manually *after* `--list` exits. Found only because I ran every command I had written down instead of trusting that I had written it correctly. |
| **Trajectory capture needed a reviewer** | The three demonstration logs each need someone to type at a blocking prompt, which makes them unreproducible by a reader and impossible to regenerate in CI. | — | Added `--decision` (plus `--edit-hs-code`). It renders the same panel, checkpoints the same state, and still reaches `GENERATE_REPORT` only through an explicit approve — but it writes `SCRIPTED DECISION ... This was not a human sign-off` into `human_notes`, so a log produced this way cannot be mistaken for one. **The interactive prompt stays the default.** A scripted reviewer still cannot introduce an HS code outside the dataset. |
| **Tested the no-invented-numbers claim instead of asserting it** | README and this file both claimed "no code path from a model token to a reported figure". That was true *by inspection*, which is not the same as true. Wrote `tests/test_report_integrity.py`: stub the model with a hostile narrative (invents 99.99% RVC, a 5% threshold, USD 1,000,000 of cost, and calls itself "a legally binding certificate of origin") and assert the assessment block is unmoved. | The isolation held — every figure still came from state, and the scan caught the fabricated ones. **But a parametrised case found a real bug:** a model returning `{"summary": null}` produced a report whose summary was the literal string `"None"`. `str(None)` is truthy, so the `narrative_ok` fallback never fired and `"None"` would have shipped as the summary of a real document. | Added a `_text()` coercion treating JSON null as absent. **The claim I was most confident about is the one where the test found a defect** — and it was in the null-handling around the guarantee, not the guarantee itself. Suite went 99 → 110 tests. |
| **Tested the checkpoint instead of trusting the control flow** | "GENERATE_REPORT is unreachable except through an approve" was a claim about an `if` statement I had written and read. Wrote `tests/test_checkpoint.py`: the whole workflow with the model stubbed by prompt shape and a scripted reviewer, asserting `reject`, a bare `edit`, and an exhausted edit loop all terminate with the report node never running. | All paths held. The edit loop is genuinely bounded at `MAX_EDIT_ROUNDS` and an edit produces a **second** `CALCULATE_RVC` trace event rather than relabelling the first. | Kept. The tests also pin the prompt shapes: the stub dispatches on prompt content and raises on anything unrecognised, so a prompt that stops asking for the shape the nodes parse now fails a test instead of failing in production. Suite 110 → 119. |
| **Documented a command that taught the wrong lesson** | Wrote the trajectory-capture commands into REPRODUCTION.md, including `M010 --decision edit --edit-hs-code 8544.42`. | M010 is a solar PV module (HS 8541.43, deliberately absent). `8544.42` is the adjacent electrical rule — **the exact wrong guess the baseline made** and the one the classification guard exists to catch. | Changed M010's demonstration to `--decision reject`, which is the correct reviewer action when no rule in the controlled set covers the product. Writing the reproduction steps carefully is what surfaced this; the code was right and the documentation was teaching people to defeat it. |
| **The HS guard is narrower than I had claimed** (most important finding) | README and this file said "the LLM cannot invent an HS code". Ran the agent on M010 expecting `CLASSIFICATION_UNAVAILABLE`. | **The agent returned `8544.42 / 12.31% / FAIL`.** The guard checks *membership in the rule table*, and `8544.42` **is** in the table — it is the adjacent insulated-conductor rule. The model proposed a plausible in-dataset neighbour and the guard passed it straight through. The baseline made the identical error. **And `VERIFY` raised no warning:** the trajectory log records a self-reported confidence of **1.00** on the wrong rule, and the low-confidence trigger fires below 0.50. **Nothing automated in the system flagged this case.** | **Rewrote the claim rather than the code.** A membership check bounds the *vocabulary* of answers, not their correctness; a self-reported confidence is not a calibrated probability — and it turned out not even to be a variable (see the row below). What actually catches M010 is the human reviewer, who sees "solar photovoltaic module" filed under "insulated electrical conductors". This is the one case in the evaluation where the human step is load-bearing rather than ceremonial — and I only know that because the case was designed to have no right answer available. A description-vs-product plausibility check would be the next thing to try, but it needs its own evidence before it earns a model call. |
| **Deterministic arithmetic is only as good as the extraction** | Agent scored 9/10 on RVC. Checked the miss. | **M007: agent 89.02% vs ground truth 87.80%.** The calculation was *correct* — on a bill of materials where one component cost had been mis-read. Status still landed on PASS, so the verdict survived; the number did not. | Recorded, not patched. Moving arithmetic into a pure function eliminates arithmetic error; it does not eliminate *input* error, and claiming otherwise would repeat the mistake in the row above. The honest framing: the workflow converts a fabrication problem into a transcription problem, which is narrower, checkable by a human against a costing sheet, and visible in the BOM printed on the review panel. |
| **The confidence score is a constant, so the guard built on it is dead** | Before submitting I went back through the trajectory logs to find the actual confidence figure behind M010, rather than repeat the README's inference from the threshold in the source. | **The model self-reported `1.00` on M010's wrong rule.** Widening the search to every record that logs the field — 4 trajectories plus their 4 checkpoints, 9 records including a synthetic one — the only values that have **ever** appeared are `1.00` from the model and `0.0` written by our own override code. Eight correct classifications and one wrong one all scored identically. | `LOW_CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD = 0.5` therefore fires **only** on the case the membership guard has already caught, and can never fire on a confident wrong answer — which is the only case where it would be worth having. A warning path that cannot trigger when it matters is not a safeguard, it is decoration. **Left in place and relabelled rather than deleted:** the panel prints it as "model self-reported", and a reviewer seeing `1.00` beside "solar module → insulated conductors" learns something true about the model that a hidden field would not teach them. Two lessons: an inference from a constant in the source is not a measurement, and this is the second time a claim I was confident about turned out narrower than written — both times found by reading the artifacts instead of the code. |

## What changed reactively vs. what was designed up front

**Designed up front:** deterministic arithmetic, deterministic lookup, typed state with
`extra="forbid"`, the `CLASSIFICATION_UNAVAILABLE` sentinel, the human interrupt.

**Changed because a run showed a problem:**
- VERIFY's origin flagging (noise on first live run → three-way classification)
- Confidence zeroing on HS override (a rejected code was carrying forward a confidence score that described a different answer)
- `_step_summary` printing a total cost that isn't populated yet at EXTRACT time
- `--list` crashed on argparse's required-source group — found by running a command I had already written into REPRODUCTION.md
- A JSON `null` narrative field shipping the literal string `"None"` as a report summary — found by the hostile-narrative test, not by reading the code

**Deliberately not built:** retry/backoff (no failures observed), LangGraph (no branching
need), cloud escalation (local model sufficient), the 1.5B model (no experiment justified
it), cryptographic signing (explicitly out of scope — the output is a draft assessment,
not a certificate).

started = time.perf_counter()
    result = call_model(
        _report_prompt(state), model=model, system=REPORT_SYSTEM, json_mode=True, temperature=0.2
    )
    elapsed = (time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000.0

    payload = parse_json_text(result.text) or {}

    def _text(key: str) -> str:
        """Coerce a narrative field to a string, treating JSON null as absent.

        ``str(None)`` is ``"None"`` -- truthy, and it would sail past the
        ``narrative_ok`` check straight into the document as the summary. Caught by
        tests/test_report_integrity.py.
        """
        value = payload.get(key)
        return "" if value is None else str(value).strip()

    narrative = {
        "summary": _text("summary"),
        "what_this_means": _text("what_this_means"),
        "recommended_next_steps": [
            str(s).strip()
            for s in (payload.get("recommended_next_steps") or [])
            if s is not None and str(s).strip()
        ],
        "limitations": _text("limitations"),
    }
    narrative_ok = bool(narrative["summary"])
    invented = _scan_for_invented_figures(narrative)

    status = state.compliance_status.value if state.compliance_status else "NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW"
    band = borderline_band_pp()

    final_output = {
        "document_title": "Draft Compliance Assessment Report — Human Approved",
        "document_type": "draft_assessment",
        "manifest_id": state.manifest_id,
        "product_description": state.product_description,
        # ---- every figure below is copied from state, never regenerated ----
        "assessment": {
            "hs_code": state.hs_code,
            "hs_code_source": (
                "selected from the controlled dataset"
                if state.is_classified
                else "not available in the controlled dataset"
            ),
            "rule_description": state.rule_description,
            "rvc_threshold_percent": state.rvc_threshold,
            "total_cost_usd": state.total_cost,
            "regionally_sourced_cost_usd": state.african_sourced_cost,
            "non_regionally_sourced_cost_usd": state.non_african_sourced_cost,
            "calculated_rvc_percent": state.calculated_rvc_percent,
            "margin_vs_threshold_pp": (
                round(state.calculated_rvc_percent - state.rvc_threshold, 2)
                if state.calculated_rvc_percent is not None and state.rvc_threshold is not None
                else None
            ),
            "borderline_band_pp": band,
            "compliance_status": status,
            "calculation_method": (
                "Build-up, materials-only cost base: regionally sourced component cost "
                "divided by total component cost. Computed by a deterministic function, "
                "not by a language model."
            ),
        },
        "bill_of_materials": [c.model_dump() for c in state.bill_of_materials],
        "human_review": {
            "decision": state.human_decision.value if state.human_decision else None,
            "reviewer_notes": state.human_notes,
            "reviewed_before_issue": True,
        },
        "narrative": narrative,
        "verification": {
            "errors": state.verification_errors,
            "warnings": verification_warnings(state),
        },
        "disclaimer": (
            "This is a draft assessment produced against a controlled set of AfCFTA "
            "rule data for guidance only. It is not a legal determination of origin, "
            "not a certificate of origin, and carries no authority. Thresholds in the "
            "underlying dataset are synthetic and illustrative. Confirm any claim with "
            "your national customs authority or a licensed customs broker before "
            "filing."
        ),
        "metadata": {
            "narrative_model": model,
            "narrative_generated": narrative_ok,
            "figures_written_by_model_in_prose": invented,
            "model_calls_this_run": state.model_call_count + 1,
        },
    }

    if not narrative_ok:
        final_output["narrative"]["summary"] = (
            "The narrative section could not be generated. The assessment figures "
            "above are unaffected: they are produced by deterministic calculation and "
            "were reviewed and approved by a human before this document was issued."
        )

    return state.logged(
        TraceEvent(
            node="GENERATE_REPORT",
            status="ok" if narrative_ok else "warn",
            model=model,
            duration_ms=elapsed,
            detail={
                "narrative_generated": narrative_ok,
                "figures_written_by_model_in_prose": invented,
                "prompt_tokens": result.prompt_tokens,
                "completion_tokens": result.completion_tokens,
            },
        )
    ).with_updates(final_output=final_output)

"""The report must not be able to carry a model-invented number.

README and CHANGELOG both claim there is no code path from a model token to a
reported figure. That claim was true by inspection; these tests make it true by
test. Each one stubs the model with a deliberately hostile narrative -- fabricated
percentages, fabricated costs, a contradicted verdict -- and asserts the assessment
block still reflects state and nothing else.

No model and no network: ``call_model`` is replaced.
"""

from decimal import Decimal

import pytest

import nodes
from llm import LlmResult
from state import ComplianceStatus, Component, HumanDecision, NavigatorState, TraceEvent

# A narrative that breaks every constraint the prompt sets: it invents an RVC
# percentage, invents a threshold, invents costs, and asserts the opposite verdict.
# Kept as valid JSON on purpose -- an unparseable payload would test the fallback
# path instead of the figure-isolation path.
HOSTILE_NARRATIVE = (
    '{"summary": "Great news: your product achieved 99.99% regional value content '
    'against a 5% threshold and is CERTIFIED as compliant.", '
    '"what_this_means": "Total cost was USD 1,000,000 of which USD 999,999 was regional.", '
    '"recommended_next_steps": ["File immediately", "Claim the 0% duty rate", '
    '"No further checks needed"], '
    '"limitations": "None. This is a legally binding certificate of origin."}'
)


def _stub_model(text: str):
    def fake_call_model(prompt, *, model, system=None, json_mode=False, temperature=0.0):
        return LlmResult(text=text, model=model, duration_ms=1.0, ok=True)

    return fake_call_model

            Component(component_name="Cocoa mass", origin_country="Ghana", cost_usd=Decimal("6000")),
            Component(component_name="Sugar", origin_country="Ghana", cost_usd=Decimal("2100")),
            Component(component_name="Foil wrap", origin_country="China", cost_usd=Decimal("2100")),
        ],
        hs_code="1806.32",
        hs_classification_confidence=0.9,
        rvc_threshold=40.0,
        rule_description="RVC of at least 40%",
        total_cost=10200.0,
        african_sourced_cost=8100.0,
        non_african_sourced_cost=2100.0,
        calculated_rvc_percent=79.41,

"""The report must not be able to carry a model-invented number.

README and CHANGELOG both claim there is no code path from a model token to a
reported figure. That claim was true by inspection; these tests make it true by
test. Each one stubs the model with a deliberately hostile narrative -- fabricated
percentages, fabricated costs, a contradicted verdict -- and asserts the assessment
block still reflects state and nothing else.

No model and no network: ``call_model`` is replaced.

### Structural guarantees, not prompt requests

Three constraints are enforced by code paths rather than asked for in prompts,
because a prompt is a request and a guard is a guarantee:

1. **The LLM cannot produce a number that reaches the report.** `GENERATE_REPORT`
   assembles every numeric field from state in Python. The model's output is confined
   to named prose fields. There is no code path from a model token to a reported
   figure. A regex scan additionally flags any figure the model writes into prose.
   This is verified by test, not by inspection: `tests/test_report_integrity.py` stubs
   the model with a narrative that invents a 99.99% RVC, a 5% threshold, a
   USD 1,000,000 cost base and calls itself a legally binding certificate — and asserts
   the assessment block is unmoved.

2. **The LLM cannot introduce an HS code from outside the dataset.** Whatever
   `CLASSIFY_HS` returns is checked for membership in the rule table; anything absent
   becomes `CLASSIFICATION_UNAVAILABLE` and routes to human review. A well-behaved
   reply and a hallucinated one are treated identically.

   **What this guard does not do — measured, not theorised.** It cannot catch a code
   that is *wrong but present in the table*. On M010 (a solar PV module, correctly
   HS 8541.43, deliberately absent from the dataset) the model proposed `8544.42` —
   insulated electrical conductors, an adjacent rule that **is** in the table. The
   guard passed it through, and the agent returned a confident `FAIL` where the
   correct answer was `NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW`. The baseline made the identical error.

   Worse: `VERIFY` raised **no warning at all** on that run. The trajectory log
   records why — the model self-reported a confidence of **1.00** on the wrong
   rule, and the low-confidence trigger fires below 0.50. Nothing automated in this
   system flagged M010.

   And the confidence score is worse than uncalibrated. Across every run where it
   was logged — four trajectories plus their checkpoints, nine records in all — the
   model returned **exactly 1.00, every time**, on the eight correct classifications
   and on the one wrong one alike. The only `0.0` in the logs is the value our own
   code writes when it overrides a code as unavailable. So the trigger can only fire
   on the case the guard has *already* caught, and never on the case it was meant to
   catch. **We shipped a warning path that cannot fire when it matters**, and I only
   know that because I went looking through the logs for the number instead of
   citing the threshold in the source.

   A membership check bounds the *vocabulary* of answers, not their correctness — and
   a self-reported confidence is not evidence of anything.

   What actually defends against this is the human checkpoint — a reviewer seeing
   "solar photovoltaic module" classified under "insulated electrical conductors"
   rejects it in a second. **This is the one case in the evaluation where the human
   step is load-bearing rather than ceremonial**, and I only learned it because we
   had built the dataset with a case that has no right answer available.

3. **No document exists without human approval.** `GENERATE_REPORT` is unreachable
   except through an explicit `approve`. State is checkpointed to disk *before* the
   pause, so the interrupt survives process exit. `tests/test_checkpoint.py` runs the
   whole workflow with the model stubbed and a scripted reviewer, and asserts that
   `reject`, a bare `edit`, and an exhausted edit loop all terminate with **no report
   node ever running** — and that the reviewer's edit re-runs the arithmetic against
   the new threshold rather than relabelling the old result.

---

You cannot instruct your way out of a failure mode whose symptom is confidence.

---

## Limitations, honestly

- **The RVC thresholds are invented.** Real AfCFTA product-specific rules live in
  Annex 2 Appendix IV and are not reproduced here. The HS codes are real; the
  thresholds are plausible synthetic values.
- **The RVC formula is simplified.** Real RVC works off ex-works price and would count
  domestic labour and overhead as regional value. This uses a materials-only cost
  base, which makes it *conservative* — it understates RVC relative to an ex-works
  basis, erring toward review rather than toward a false PASS. Because the cost base
  is exactly the bill of materials, the build-up and build-down methods are
  algebraically identical here, so the choice of method cannot change a verdict.
- **Ten HS codes, not the full nomenclature.** Anything outside them correctly
  returns `CLASSIFICATION_UNAVAILABLE` rather than a guess — but only if the model
  proposes something outside them. It may instead propose a wrong code that is inside
  the table, which the guard cannot detect (see M010 above).
- **The self-reported confidence score is worthless as a signal.** In every run we
  logged it, the model returned `1.00` — on right answers and on M010's wrong one
  equally. It is presented on the review panel labelled "model self-reported" so a
  reviewer discounts it accordingly, and the low-confidence trigger built on top of it
  has never fired on a case that needed it. Removing it would be defensible; keeping it
  visible and labelled is what we chose, because a reviewer who sees `1.00` beside
  "solar photovoltaic module → insulated electrical conductors" learns something true
  about the model.
- **Origin is taken at face value.** The system does not verify that a component
  claimed as Ghanaian actually originates in Ghana. That is a documentary question.
- **No cumulation rules, no de minimis, no tariff-shift criteria.** Real RoO offers
  several routes to qualification; this implements the RVC route only.
- **Single-user CLI.** No auth, no multi-tenancy, no audit trail beyond local logs.

## Where this goes next without a rewrite

The seam is already in the right place. `LOOKUP_RULE` reads a local JSON file behind a
typed interface; pointing it at a real tariff database changes one function. The
origin list is data, not code. `run_pipeline_to_verify` is already separated from the
human step, so a web or API frontend would call the same function and render the same
review panel to a queue of reviewers instead of a terminal. Nothing here assumes a
terminal except the decision provider, which is already an injectable callable.

---

## Repository layout

   needs it, and nothing automated caught M010. But it needs its own evidence before it
   earns a model call — and, given guard 2's history, before I would claim it works.

lines: | **The HS guard is narrower than I had claimed** (most important finding) | README and this file said "the LLM cannot invent an HS code". Ran the agent on M010 expecting `CLASSIFICATION_UNAVAILABLE`. | **The agent returned `8544.42 / 12.31% / FAIL`.** The guard checks *membership in the rule table*, and `8544.42` **is** in the table — it is the adjacent insulated-conductor rule. The model proposed a plausible in-dataset neighbour and the guard passed it straight through. The baseline made the identical error. **And `VERIFY` raised no warning:** the trajectory log records a self-reported confidence of **1.00** on the wrong rule, and the low-confidence trigger fires below 0.50. **Nothing automated in the system flagged this case.** | **Rewrote the claim rather than the code.** A membership check bounds the *vocabulary* of answers, not their correctness; a self-reported confidence is not a calibrated probability — and it turned out not even to be a variable (see the row below). What actually catches M010 is the human reviewer, who sees "solar photovoltaic module" filed under "insulated electrical conductors". This is the one case in the evaluation where the human step is load-bearing rather than ceremonial — and I only know that because the case was designed to have no right answer available. A description-vs-product plausibility check would be the next thing to try, but it needs its own evidence before it earns a model call. |

| **Deterministic arithmetic is only as good as the extraction** | Agent scored 9/10 on RVC. Checked the miss. | **M007: agent 89.02% vs ground truth 87.80%.** The calculation was *correct* — on a bill of materials where one component cost had been mis-read. Status still landed on PASS, so the verdict survived; the number did not. | Recorded, not patched. Moving arithmetic into a pure function eliminates arithmetic error; it does not eliminate *input* error, and claiming otherwise would repeat the mistake in the row above. The honest framing: the workflow converts a fabrication problem into a transcription problem, which is narrower, checkable by a human against a costing sheet, and visible in the BOM printed on the review panel. |

## VIDEO SCRIPT (≤ 5 min)

Steps 4, 5 and 6 above are your rehearsal — they are the same commands you record.

**Setup before recording:** large terminal font, model already warm (step 2), and have
the M010 command ready to paste.

### 0:00–0:35 — The problem

Show a raw manifest on screen (`python src/graph.py --list`, then open
`data/synthetic_manifests.json`).

> "A chocolate maker in Accra has a product and a bill of materials. Under AfCFTA, they
> get a lower tariff only if enough of the product's value comes from the region — and
> the threshold depends on their HS code. Finding out means reading tariff schedules
> written for customs professionals, or paying a broker. On a ten-thousand-dollar batch,
> the cost of finding out rivals the benefit of knowing. So a lot of exporters just don't
> claim what they're entitled to."

### 0:35–1:30 — The baseline fails, confidently

Run step 4. Ten responses on screen.

> "Here's one zero-shot prompt doing the whole job. Ten cases, and every answer is three
> bare lines with no working. M008 says twenty-seven point six nine percent — the truth is
> sixty-seven point three two, and it said FAIL when the answer was PASS.
>
> Now look at M002 and M010. Byte-identical. Thirty-seven point zero zero percent for
> both. One is a Moroccan wiring harness, the other's a South African solar module —
> different components, different origins, different total cost. It wasn't calculating. It
> was matching a plausible percentage to an HS code."

**Say the fairness point out loud — this is a good-faith signal judges look for:**

> "And to be clear, I gave the baseline the full rule table in its prompt. My thresholds
> are synthetic, so withholding them would have guaranteed a zero and rigged my own
> comparison."

### 1:30–2:20 — The structural fix

Show the architecture diagram in README. Point at which nodes are the model and which are
pure Python.

> "So the model never touches a number that reaches the report. It reads messy text and it
> writes prose. Every figure is assembled from state in Python. There's no code path from
> a model token to a reported number."

Run `python -m pytest tests/ -q`.

> "A hundred and nineteen tests in half a second, no model needed. One of them feeds the
> model a narrative that invents a ninety-nine point nine nine percent RVC and calls itself
> a legally binding certificate — and asserts the document comes out unmoved."

Show the scorecard.

> "RVC accuracy goes from zero out of ten to nine out of ten. It costs 2.6× the latency and
> twice the model calls. That's a real trade, not a free win."

### 2:20–3:25 — M010 live (the centrepiece)

Run step 5. Let the nodes print.

> "This is a solar photovoltaic module. Its correct code is 8541.43, and I deliberately
> left that out of the dataset — so the right answer is 'I can't classify this, send it to
> a human.'
>
> That's not what happens. The model proposes 8544.42 — insulated electrical conductors.
> An adjacent rule that *is* in my table. So my membership guard passes it straight
> through, and you get a confident FAIL.
>
> And look — zero warnings. Confidence one point zero zero. I went through every log
> before submitting: it says one point zero zero on every single case, right or wrong. So
> the low-confidence trigger I built on top of it has never once fired when it mattered.
> Nothing automated in this system caught this case."

Type `reject`.

> "The only thing that catches it is a person reading 'photovoltaic module' next to
> 'insulated electrical conductors'. And no report is produced at all. This is the one case
> in my evaluation where the human step is load-bearing instead of ceremonial."

### 3:25–4:00 — Second proof point

> "One more. I wrote a test to verify the claim I was *most* confident about — that no
> model output can reach a reported figure. The isolation held. But the test found a
> different bug: when the model returned a JSON null for the summary, Python stringified it
> to the literal word 'None', which is truthy, so the fallback never fired and 'None' would
> have shipped as the summary of a real document.

>   arithmetic was. Opening on a case where the model got the *easy* part right is far
>   more persuasive than opening on one where it got everything wrong.

>   said 27.69%, FAIL. A **39.63 pp** error, in the direction that costs the exporter
>   money — they abandon a preference claim they were entitled to.

>   **carton from Tema, Ghana that counts toward Nigerian regional content**. Cross-border
>   regional sourcing is the entire point of the agreement, visible in one bill of
>   materials.

>   versus "it passes at 67.32%" is as stark as this dataset gets.

> Edo State, caustic soda from China, a shipping carton from Tema in Ghana. Under AfCFTA
> they get a lower tariff only if enough of the product's value comes from the region —
> and the threshold depends on their HS code. Finding out means reading tariff schedules
> written for customs professionals, or paying a broker. On a four-thousand-dollar batch,
> the cost of finding out rivals the benefit of knowing. So a lot of exporters just don't
> claim what they're entitled to."

Run step 4. Ten responses on screen.

> "Here's one zero-shot prompt doing the whole job. Ten cases, three bare lines each, no
> working shown.
>

> point six nine percent, and FAIL. The truth is sixty-seven point three two against a
> thirty percent threshold. That's a PASS it called a FAIL — a thirty-nine point six point
> error, and the exporter walks away from a claim they were entitled to. M004, the Kano
> handbags, is the same story.
>

> both. One is a Moroccan wiring harness, the other's a South African solar module —
> different components, different origins, different total cost. It wasn't calculating. It
> was matching a plausible percentage to an HS code."

> are synthetic, so withholding them would have guaranteed a zero and rigged my own
> comparison."

Show the architecture diagram in README. Point at which nodes are the model and which are
pure Python.

> "So the model never touches a number that reaches the report. It reads messy text and it
> writes prose. Every figure is assembled from state in Python. There's no code path from
> a model token to a reported number."

Run `python -m pytest tests/ -q`.

> "A hundred and twenty-seven tests in under two seconds, no model needed. One of them feeds
> the model a narrative that invents a ninety-nine point nine nine percent RVC and calls
> itself a legally binding certificate — and asserts the document comes out unmoved."

Show the scorecard.

> "RVC accuracy goes from zero out of ten to nine out of ten. It costs 2.6× the latency and
> twice the model calls. That's a real trade, not a free win."

> "This is a solar photovoltaic module. Its correct code is 8541.43, and I deliberately
> left that out of the dataset — so the right answer is 'I can't classify this, send it to
> a human.'
>

> through, and you get a confident FAIL.

> the low-confidence trigger I built on top of it has never once fired when it mattered.
> Nothing automated in this system caught this case."

Type `reject`.

> "The only thing that catches it is a person reading 'photovoltaic module' next to
> 'insulated electrical conductors'. And no report is produced at all. This is the one case
> in my evaluation where the human step is load-bearing instead of ceremonial."

### 3:25–4:00 — Second proof point: two claims I was wrong about

running long, cut this section to the single bolded sentence at the end.

> certified or cleared by any authority. Then I actually read a report it produced,
> instead of checking that it produced one. It said: 'You can now export your chocolate
> bars without any issues related to trade regulations.' Three lines above my own

>

> the model wrote perfectly well — was generated on every single run and never rendered.

>
> So the claims now get the same treatment the numbers already had: scanned, flagged,
> and the warning printed *above* the prose, because a caveat after the claim isn't a
> caveat."

**Option B — the null-string bug.**

> "I wrote a test to verify the claim I was *most* confident about — that no model output
> can reach a reported figure. The isolation held. But the test found a different bug:
> when the model returned a JSON null for the summary, Python stringified it to the
> literal word 'None', which is truthy, so the fallback never fired and 'None' would have
> shipped as the summary of a real document."

Close either option on this:

> **"Every claim in this project that turned out narrower than I'd written it, I found by
> reading an artifact — a log, a raw response, a finished document. Not one of them by

## The user and the bottleneck

**Who:** A small manufacturer or exporter — a chocolate maker in Accra, a knitwear
factory in Athi River, a soap works in Sapele. They have a product and they know
what goes into it: components, where each one came from, what each one cost.

**What they need:** Under AfCFTA, a product only gets preferential tariff treatment
if enough of its value originates in the region. "Enough" is a percentage threshold
that depends on the product's HS code. Meet it and you pay a lower duty; miss it and
you don't.

**Why it's hard today:** Finding out means reading tariff schedules written for
customs professionals, correctly classifying your own product into a six-digit HS
code, locating the rule that governs it, and doing the value arithmetic — or paying a
customs broker for a few hours of their time. For a firm shipping a $10,000 batch,
the cost of finding out can rival the benefit of knowing. So many simply don't claim
the preference they're entitled to.

**What this does:** Reads the manifest as the exporter would actually write it,
identifies the applicable rule from the controlled dataset, computes the regional
value content **deterministically**, and shows a reviewer the numbers *before*
producing anything. Under a minute of compute instead of a broker's invoice.

Done. Nigerian example first, then the fix your run exposed.

## Yes — switch to M008, and not only for geography

M008 is **Sapele Soap Works, Sapele** — and it's the stronger opener on the merits:

| | |
|---|---|
| Baseline said | `3401.11 / 27.69% / FAIL` |
| Truth | `3401.11 / 67.32% / PASS` (30% threshold) |
| Error | **39.63 pp, verdict inverted** |

**The HS code is correct.** That's why it's the better opening case than M001 — you show the model getting the *easy* part right and still inverting the answer, which is the whole thesis in one case. Opening on a total failure is weaker than opening on a partial one.

It also already *is* your hot take's example, so video and README agree. And the manifest itself tells the AfCFTA story: palm kernel oil from Edo State, plus a **carton from Tema, Ghana that counts toward Nigerian regional content** — cross-border sourcing visible in one bill of materials.

M004 (**Kano Leatherworks, Kano** — handbags, `4202.21`, truth 62.78% vs 45% PASS, baseline said 37.50% FAIL) is your backup. Same shape, right code, inverted verdict. One clause, don't run it.

Script rewritten in [TODO-BEFORE-SUBMIT.md](TODO-BEFORE-SUBMIT.md), including a rehearsal note for step 4.

## The overclaim is fixed

Your pasted run shipped a legal assurance, and it turned out to be two defects:

1. `_scan_for_overclaims` in [src/nodes.py](src/nodes.py) — the structural twin of the figure scan. Phrase list, negation guard so *"this is **not** a certificate of origin"* stays legal, hits into `claims_flagged_in_prose` and the trace, node status → `warn`.
2. **`limitations` was never rendered.** Generated on every run since the node was written, present in the prompt and the JSON, dropped by `render_report`. The model had written a genuinely good caveat — *"does not constitute a legal determination"* — and nobody could read it.

The warning prints **above** the summary. A caveat after the claim isn't a caveat:

```
  !! READ THE NARRATIVE BELOW WITH CARE
  ----------------------------------------------------------------
    - summary: 'meet the criteria to be exported' — asserts export eligibility broader…
    - what_this_means: 'without any issues' — unqualified assurance
    - what_this_means: 'You can now export' — grants a permission this system cannot grant
  Disregard those phrasings. This document authorises nothing.
```

The wording is quoted rather than scrubbed, so the reviewer sees what the model tried to say.

Two things worth flagging honestly, both now in the README: it's a phrase list, so like the HS guard it bounds *recognised phrasings*, not meaning — one of my own test assertions failed because I'd asserted a hit the list didn't make. And `GENERATE_REPORT` runs **after** the checkpoint, so the reviewer approves figures and never reads prose; the scan stands in for a review rather than replacing one. Moving generation before the pause is now the top item in "Where this goes next."

**`127 passed`** (was 119). Eight new tests — one stubs the model with the verbatim narrative from your trajectory log, one asserts a careful narrative *isn't* flagged, one asserts the warning appears before `SUMMARY`.

**Keep that fifth log.** `M001-20260829-142355.json` is now cited by name in the test and in REPRODUCTION §8 — deleting it breaks a test and orphans a documented claim.

CHANGELOG row 40 is written, and it makes the pattern explicit: this is the third claim that turned out narrower than written, and all three were found by reading an artifact — a log, a raw response, a finished document. None by reading code. That's a better close for §3:25 than the null-string bug, so the script offers both with that one recommended.

Remaining: record, then commit and push — still blocked on you creating the repo and giving me the URL, since `gh` isn't installed.

## 9. Timing notes (measured, not estimated)

- **First call after `ollama serve` takes ~25 s** even for a two-token reply — that

  ran 33–45 s for real work.

input.new_string:
## 9. Timing notes (measured, not estimated)

Measured on a Windows 11 machine running the 7B model on local hardware, across the six
committed trajectory logs plus the two evaluation runs. Yours will differ; the *relative*
comparison between the two systems is what the evaluation is about.

| | Model calls | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline, per case | 1 | **37.8 s** avg over 10 cases |
| **Graded workflow pipeline** (`EXTRACT` → `VERIFY`) | 2 | **97.7 s** avg over 10 cases — this is the figure in the README's results table |
| Full run you **approve** (adds `GENERATE_REPORT`) | 3 | **158 s – 339 s** wall clock across the five approved trajectories |
| Full run you **reject** | 2 | **85 s** (M010) |

**Budget three to five minutes for an interactive run, not ninety seconds.** The 97.7 s
figure is honest but it measures the *graded* pipeline, which stops at the human
checkpoint. Adding the narrative call roughly doubles it.

Per-node latency, min–max across the six trajectories:

| Node | Range | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `EXTRACT` | **68–169 s** | Consistently the most expensive call: longest prompt, longest structured output |
| `CLASSIFY_HS` | **14–82 s** | Short output, but the shortlist makes the prompt large |
| `GENERATE_REPORT` | **69–88 s** | Only runs on approve |
| `LOOKUP_RULE`, `CALCULATE_RVC`, `VERIFY` | **0.0 s** | Pure Python. They appear as `0.0s` in the logs because they are single-digit milliseconds |

**Same node, same machine, same model, 2.5× spread.** `CLASSIFY_HS` ran 14 s on one run
and 82 s on another; `EXTRACT` 68 s and 169 s. That is memory pressure and model
eviction on a laptop, not workload — nothing in the prompt changed. It is also why the
one thing this project measured carelessly was latency: see CHANGELOG's "Two eval runs
raced each other". **Do not run anything else against Ollama while timing.**

- **Cold start is worse than a single number suggests.** A first trivial call after
  `ollama serve` returns in ~25 s, but the first *real* run of the workflow after a cold
  start took **339 s** — `EXTRACT` alone was 169 s. Warm the model with a throwaway run
  before you time anything or record anything.

lines: | **The HS guard is narrower than I had claimed** (most important finding) | README and this file said "the LLM cannot invent an HS code". Ran the agent on M010 expecting `CLASSIFICATION_UNAVAILABLE`. | **The agent returned `8544.42 / 12.31% / FAIL`.** The guard checks *membership in the rule table*, and `8544.42` **is** in the table — it is the adjacent insulated-conductor rule. The model proposed a plausible in-dataset neighbour and the guard passed it straight through. The baseline made the identical error. **And `VERIFY` raised no warning:** the trajectory log records a self-reported confidence of **1.00** on the wrong rule, and the low-confidence trigger fires below 0.50. **Nothing automated in the system flagged this case.** | **Rewrote the claim rather than the code.** A membership check bounds the *vocabulary* of answers, not their correctness; a self-reported confidence is not a calibrated probability — and it turned out not even to be a variable (see the row below). What actually catches M010 is the human reviewer, who sees "solar photovoltaic module" filed under "insulated electrical conductors". This is the one case in the evaluation where the human step is load-bearing rather than ceremonial — and I only know that because the case was designed to have no right answer available. A description-vs-product plausibility check would be the next thing to try, but it needs its own evidence before it earns a model call. |

| **Deterministic arithmetic is only as good as the extraction** | Agent scored 9/10 on RVC. Checked the miss. | **M007: agent 89.02% vs ground truth 87.80%.** The calculation was *correct* — on a bill of materials where one component cost had been mis-read. Status still landed on PASS, so the verdict survived; the number did not. | Recorded, not patched. Moving arithmetic into a pure function eliminates arithmetic error; it does not eliminate *input* error, and claiming otherwise would repeat the mistake in the row above. The honest framing: the workflow converts a fabrication problem into a transcription problem, which is narrower, checkable by a human against a costing sheet, and visible in the BOM printed on the review panel. |

| **The confidence score is a constant, so the guard built on it is dead** | Before submitting I went back through the trajectory logs to find the actual confidence figure behind M010, rather than repeat the README's inference from the threshold in the source. | **The model self-reported `1.00` on M010's wrong rule.** Widening the search to every record that logs the field — 4 trajectories plus their 4 checkpoints, 9 records including a synthetic one — the only values that have **ever** appeared are `1.00` from the model and `0.0` written by our own override code. Eight correct classifications and one wrong one all scored identically. | `LOW_CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD = 0.5` therefore fires **only** on the case the membership guard has already caught, and can never fire on a confident wrong answer — which is the only case where it would be worth having.
